issues.issue: Item 1 names the insured as "Children's Health Systems, Inc.", but General Amendatory Endorsement No. 8 (c125) amends Item 1 to read "Children's Health System, Inc." A court could be asked which entity is the Named Insured, and hence which entities take coverage through the Named Insured definition (c028).

"Hospital" as the stated business of the Named Insured is undifferentiated: it does not say whether the risk is a children's hospital, a teaching hospital or a general acute-care hospital. That characterization is what other instruments in the file turn on, and the declaration gives no boundary for it.

Item 3 states $18,000,000 each occurrence and $9,000,000 aggregate, but General Amendatory Endorsement No. 4 (c118) amends the policy limits to $20,000,000 each occurrence and $20,000,000 aggregate. A court would have to decide which set of limits governs.

The declared aggregate limit ($9,000,000) is half the declared each-occurrence limit ($18,000,000), so the aggregate cap is smaller than a single covered occurrence. The two figures cannot both be given their ordinary effect under Insuring Agreement III (c017).

"[N]ot less than short rate of earned premium as the minimum premium" fixes no ascertainable figure or short-rate table, so the minimum retained premium on cancellation cannot be computed from the policy. The term "short rate" is undefined.

The Schedule of Underlying Insurance lists only CGL, automobile and employers liability, with no hospital professional liability policy, yet the Contingent Excess Medical Malpractice endorsement (c108) applies "directly over the underlying insurance listed in this policy and identified as being listed for contingency coverage purposes" and the Aggregate Limits Endorsement (c093) presupposes a professional liability hazard. Nothing in Item 7 answers those cross-references.

The insuring agreement grants indemnity only for "personal injury, property damage or advertising liability," with no grant for professional or medical malpractice liability, yet the Aggregate Limits Endorsement (c093), the Contingent Excess Medical Malpractice endorsement (c106-c110) and the Policy Territory endorsements (c111, c119) all assume hospital professional liability coverage exists under this policy. The scope of the grant can only be settled by reading the endorsements against this clause.

The defense obligation attaches only to an occurrence "not covered by any underlying coverage described in the schedule of underlying insurance or any other underlying insurance collectible by the insured," and "collectible" is not defined. Whether coverage that an underlying insurer disputes or denies is nonetheless "collectible" decides whether the drop-down defense duty arises.

This paragraph withholds defense and legal expenses "covered by underlying insurance," which cannot be squared cleanly with the Supplementary Payments obligation in c010 or with the assumption-of-defense duty in c012 when underlying limits are disputed or eroded. Which clause governs a partially covered defense is left open.

The trigger is that the underlying limits be "exhausted by an occurrence," but the policy nowhere says whether exhaustion means payment in full by the underlying insurer, a below-limits settlement, or the insured's own payment. Read with Loss Payable (c054) and Maintenance of Underlying Insurance (c062), the meaning of exhaustion is contestable.

This clause makes supplementary payments payable "in addition to the ultimate net loss," while the definition of ultimate net loss (c032) already excludes all loss and legal expenses and Limit of Liability (c016) caps liability at the Item 3 amount. Whether defense costs sit outside the limits turns on reconciling the three.

"[P]revented by law or otherwise from carrying out this agreement" contains an open-ended "or otherwise" that has no ascertainable boundary next to the specific reference to law. The clause also leaves unclear which expenses the company must then pay.

The insured must reimburse the company for loss paid "within the self insured retention stated in item 4," but the Retained Limit definition (c033) makes the Item 4 retention operative only when underlying insurance is inapplicable. Whether the $10,000 retention applies in addition to the underlying limits is not resolved between the two.

This limit refers to "the amount stated in Item 3 of the declarations," which General Amendatory Endorsement No. 4 (c118) purports to change while calling it "Item 2." The amount this clause imports is therefore contested.

The aggregate limit here bites only on loss "arising out of the products or completed operations hazards," whereas the Aggregate Limits Endorsement (c093) adds "or any professional liability hazard." Which aggregate applies to a malpractice-type loss cannot be settled from this paragraph alone.

This clause says the policy applies to occurrences happening anywhere, while the two Policy Territory Amended endorsements (c111 and c119) purport to amend "the Policy Territory provisions of the Hospital Professional Liability coverage part attached to the policy." Whether those endorsements modify this territory clause, or a coverage part that is not in this instrument, is open.

This exclusion of "loss of use of tangible property which has not been physically injured or destroyed" cuts directly against limb (2) of the Property Damage definition (c035), which expressly includes such loss of use. The two must be reconciled to know what loss-of-use claims are covered.

The Named Insured definition automatically sweeps in "any subsidiary" and any other organization under the named insured's control, while the Additional Named Insureds endorsement (c094) states that "no automatic coverage for entities newly acquired by any of them is extended hereby." Whether a newly acquired or controlled affiliate is insured turns on which of the two governs.

This paragraph's pollution exclusion, with its "sudden and accidental" exception, is the very exclusion the Total Pollution Exclusion (c099) says it "replaces," and the two describe the excluded substances differently. Which text governs a pollution claim requires reading them together.

Sub-paragraph (5) makes any person insured under an underlying policy an insured here "subject to all the limitations upon coverage under such policy," while General Amendatory Endorsement No. 1 (c096) grants additional-insured status "only with respect to their interest in the operations of the Named Insured." The status of a lessor or lender named in c096 depends on which limitation controls.

"Ultimate net loss" is defined as the sum "actually paid or payable" in settlement or satisfaction, and those two words point in opposite directions on whether the insured must have disbursed money before the company indemnifies. Loss Payable (c054) compounds the question by requiring payment of the underlying limit first.

"Retained Limit" is the "greater of" the total underlying limits or the Item 4 self-insured retention, which leaves it unclear whether the $10,000 retention applies in addition to, or only in the absence of, collectible underlying insurance. The clause's own proviso ("if the insurance afforded by the underlying insurance is inapplicable") pulls against the "greater of" formula.

This definition of Personal Injury expressly includes mental anguish, shock, false arrest, libel, slander and invasion of privacy, and (5) racial or religious discrimination, all of which the Personal Injury Endorsement (c064) and the Exclusion of Discrimination (c087) strike out. What "personal injury" means in the insuring agreement (c009) cannot be read off this clause alone.

Limb (1) requires the physical injury to "occur during the policy period" while limb (2) requires only that the loss of use be caused by an occurrence during the period, producing two different triggers within one definition. In a progressive-damage claim the choice of limb decides coverage.

"Occurrence" requires injury "neither expected nor intended from the standpoint of the insured," a subjective-intent standard that is undefined and is applied across multiple insureds under c028-c031. Whether one insured's expectation defeats coverage for others is not addressed.

"[A]ll such exposure to substantially the same general conditions existing at or emanating from one location or source shall be deemed one occurrence" gives no measure for "substantially the same" or for what counts as a single "source." The number of occurrences drives the each-occurrence limit in c016.

The products hazard is stated to include "personal injury and property damage," but the operative proviso then speaks only of "bodily injury or property damage," a term the policy does not define. The mismatch narrows or widens the hazard depending on which phrase is read as controlling.

Notice is due "as soon as practicable" once it "appears that an occurrence is likely to involve indemnity under this policy," and neither the trigger nor the deadline has any fixed content. The point at which the insured's duty crystallises on an excess policy is exactly what a late-notice defence would be fought over.

Liability is said not to attach until the underlying limit "has been paid by or on behalf of the insured," which cannot be squared with Maintenance of Underlying Insurance (c062), under which the policy applies as though unmaintained underlying policies were in force. Whether an unpaid or uncollectible underlying limit blocks attachment is left unresolved.

This Action Against Company condition, including the no-privity sentence, is deleted in its entirety by the Wisconsin Amendatory Endorsement (c074-c076), which substitutes a shorter text permitting "any person or organization" to recover. Whether any part of this clause survives is a live question.

The assignment sentence is incomplete: it says assignment "shall not bind" without stating whom it does not bind or what consent is required, and then runs into an unrelated clause about the unexpired portion of the policy period. As written the restriction has no ascertainable operation.

This clause makes the policy excess over any other valid and collectible insurance "whether or not described in the Schedule of Underlying Insurance," which pulls against the Retained Limit definition (c033) fixing the attachment point by reference to scheduled limits plus other collectible underlying insurance. Whether unscheduled insurance raises the attachment point or merely shares loss is unclear.

The apportionment order set out here reimburses interests that paid in excess of the retained limit first and the company second, but the Wisconsin Subrogation amendment (c077) says the company recovers "only after the insured has been fully compensated for damages." The two orders of priority cannot both be applied.

This clause says notice to or knowledge of any agent shall not effect a waiver or estop the company, while the Wisconsin Changes endorsement (c078) provides that an agent's knowledge of a fact breaching a condition is the company's knowledge and shall not void the policy. The two provisions are in direct opposition on agent knowledge.

This condition requires thirty days' written notice of cancellation by the company, while the Cancellation - Wisconsin endorsement (c069-c071) allows ten days and General Amendatory Endorsement No. 3 (c098) requires sixty days. Which notice period governs a cancellation is a direct conflict among three provisions.

The warranty to maintain underlying policies, with the saving clause that the policy applies as if they had been maintained, sits against Loss Payable (c054) and the Retained Limit definition (c033), which condition attachment on actual payment of the underlying limit. The consequence of an unmaintained or exhausted underlying policy differs depending on which clause is applied.

"Except insofar as coverage is available to the insured in the underlying insurance listed" is grammatically incomplete — listed where, and on what date — and it is unclear whether the following-form carve-back tracks the Item 7 schedule or any underlying policy actually in force. The scope of the contractual liability exclusion turns on that missing referent.

The endorsement preserves coverage "insofar as coverage is afforded under the underlying insurance or self insured retention listed in Item 7 of the Declarations," but Item 7 is the Schedule of Underlying Insurance and the self-insured retention is stated in Item 4. The mis-citation leaves the carve-back's reach uncertain.
